claim: The simplest workshop-suitable apps for absolute beginners are single-purpose, single-screen tools (dice roller, decision maker, tip calculator, color generator, text-case converter) buildable in 10-15 minutes with no database persistence.
quote: Single-purpose functionality; Completable in one sitting; Minimal user input requirements; Simple, immediate visual feedback; No database persistence needed.

claim: Features that consistently blow up beginner scope include email delivery, OAuth/identity, image/video generation, native mobile, and enterprise security; authentication remains a weak point across all vibe-coding platforms.
quote: Email systems: Building reliable, consistent email delivery that won't break or get flagged as spam requires significant infrastructure work. OAuth/identity management: Authentication remains a weak point across platforms... Native mobile apps: Complexity multiplies significantly versus web apps

claim: Hackathon facilitators report scope is the single biggest demoralizer; the facilitator's role is explicitly to help participants narrow scope and prioritize, and visual/user-facing features should be prioritized over backend depth.
quote: Participants try to tackle everything possible, setting the scope way too big to accomplish something meaningful... help the participants to narrow the scope and prioritize... Visual elements are more appealing than looking at code or backend things

claim: At Singapore's 65labs workshop, instructor Sherry Jiang stresses vibe-coding suits very simple, lightweight consumer apps and emphasizes shipping speed over polish — starting over is often smarter than patching.
quote: Building is so fast now that it's often smarter to start over than to patch a messy product... vibe coding is best suited to very simple, lightweight, straightforward consumer apps—not anything very technical that will require heavy enterprise security.

claim: Tool selection maps to scope: v0 or Tempo for a single UI component or landing page; Lovable, Bolt, or Replit only when user accounts and stored data are required — i.e., layman workshops should stay on the lighter end.
quote: For a single UI component or landing page, v0 or Tempo are recommended. A complete application with user accounts and stored data requires a full-stack builder: Lovable, Bolt, or Replit.

claim: Even a 'simple' Pomodoro reached 90% in three days but consumed months on the last 10% once OAuth, accessibility, performance, and database wiring entered scope; the lesson is force MVP to one primary loop and one settings screen.
quote: the last 10% isn't 10%... Force an MVP: Build one primary loop and one settings screen; defer everything else... OAuth configuration, database connections, and package management proved harder than anticipated

claim: Five-minute up-front documentation of features, user types, and main screens prevents hours of redirects; common beginner failures are vague prompts, prompt overload, contradictory features, and skipping iteration.
quote: Spending five minutes documenting what you're building—features, user types, and main screens—prevents hours of redirects and rework later... Dumping entire wish lists into single massive requests overwhelms the model

claim: Stanford's non-developer Lovable workshop scopes outputs to a 'to-do list or feedback form' with four modules — first page, design, interactivity, publish — explicitly excluding traditional coding prerequisites.
quote: Learners create real, working web projects using Lovable.dev, including examples like a to-do list or feedback form... no coding or web design experience required

claim: Lovable can persist beginner-app data via browser local storage instead of a backend database, which removes auth/server complexity but loses cross-device sync — exactly the trade-off appropriate for a 2-3 hour session.
quote: Lovable can use local storage, which stores the data in a local browser database. This method has the advantage of not requiring an internet connection but also has the disadvantage of not sharing data across devices.

claim: Over 60% of security issues in vibe-coded apps come from missing row-level security, exposed API keys, client-side-only auth, and IDOR — i.e., as soon as you add login/multi-user you import a class of problems beginners cannot debug in a workshop.
quote: the most common vulnerabilities are missing database access controls (RLS), exposed API keys in frontend code, client-side only authentication, and insecure direct object references (IDOR), which account for over 60% of all security issues found in vibe-coded applications

claim: Successful non-developer vibe-coded projects cluster around low-complexity utilities (plywood cutting visualizer, SEO calculator, tip-style tools) that are single-user with no persistence — the same shape that fits a 2-3 hour session.
quote: Plywood Cutting Visualizer | Justin Lai | Claude | Utility tool | Low | Input dimensions, calculate cuts, show scraps | Single | No

claim: Recommended beginner project shape is a Todo or Quiz app — 'small enough to finish in an afternoon, complex enough to teach real patterns' — with concretely specified UI (4 multiple-choice answers, score counter, 30-second countdown).
quote: The Todo App or Quiz App are ideal starting points — small enough to finish in an afternoon, complex enough to teach real patterns... Build a quiz component with 4 multiple-choice answers, a score counter in the top right, and a 30-second countdown timer
